svg.aria-label: Diagram: service account impersonation as a two-identity exchange compared with keys and attached service accounts, what each records in audit logs, the permission required, the one hour default token lifetime extendable to twelve hours, and the attached service account route that reopens the non-repudiation gap
svg.title: Impersonation: two identities in, two identities in the log
svg.text: A key asks a service to verify a secret. Impersonation asks an already-identified principal.
So the request cannot be made anonymously even in principle. That is what the audit trail is reporting.
Three ways to act as a service account — and two of them record the same thing
Route
Identities
What the audit log shows
Impersonation
TWO
most logs: the principal AND the account
A service account key
one
only the service account
An ATTACHED service account
one
only the service account
Google’s hedge is worth keeping: MOST audit logs, not all. Verify it for the API you depend on.
The catch: a total key ban closes row 2 and leaves row 3 untouched
Enforce disableServiceAccountKeyCreation (#40), migrate every workload, delete the last key file —
and a developer with an SSH session to a VM still acts as its attached service account.
Google lists this BESIDE keys, not as a footnote: executing code on privileged resources can
create privilege-escalation and non-repudiation risks.
The control is not a credential policy. It is who can get a shell on which machines.
The exchange
An authenticated principal gets a token for the
account, then authenticates as it.
Needs iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken
— which IS everything that account can do.
Review it like a direct grant.
What you get, in time
Default maximum token lifetime: 1 hour (3,600s).
Extendable to 12 hours (43,200s) — per account,
via a LIST constraint naming who gets it.
Not automatically refreshed. The expiry forces the
exchange to repeat — and re-present the human.
Why the expiry matters, and it is not blast radius
A key contains no trace of the human, so “who” is unanswerable by construction.
In impersonation the human is not an annotation on the request — they are a prerequisite for it.
So a token that expires is what keeps the two-identity structure TRUE OVER TIME.
And you cannot do it in the console — there you always authenticate with your user credentials. CLI and API only.
An attached service account is correct for a workload: the machine IS the account, one identity, nothing missing.
It becomes a problem only when a human gets inside the machine. The boundary is an identity acting versus being worn.
